nodes.label: Hackett et al. (1973) described a metabolic myopathy associated with chronic lactic acidemia, growth failure, and nerve deafness.

Mastaglia et al. (1980) described a 23-year-old man with mitochondrial myopathy who had a high-output circulatory state and cardiomyopathy that caused cardiac insufficiency 22 years before the skeletal myopathy appeared. Venous lactate levels were elevated, and at one stage of the illness he developed severe lactic acidosis.

In the patient reported by Mastaglia et al. (1980), electron microscopy of muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and an accumulation of neutral lipids. The lipid accumulation was confirmed by histochemistry and thin-layer chromatography.
Mastaglia et al. (1980) observed a marked improvement in their patient's myopathy after he started prednisone and thiamine. The improvement continued after both drugs were withdrawn.

Mastaglia et al. (1980) did not define the metabolic defect in their patient. They postulated an abnormality involving the Krebs cycle that resulted in overproduction of lactate and lipid accumulation in muscle.

Mancuso et al. (2009) found that iPLA2-gamma-null mice (iPLA2-gamma -/-) had major changes in hippocampal phospholipid metabolism and mitochondrial phospholipid homeostasis. Shotgun lipidomics showed a markedly raised hippocampal cardiolipin content, with the molecular species shifted toward shorter chains. The mice also had altered choline and ethanolamine glycerophospholipids, including less plasmenylethanolamine, along with more oxidized phosphatidylethanolamine species and more ceramides.

In iPLA2-gamma-null mice, Mancuso et al. (2009) saw enlarged, heteromorphic lamellar structures undergoing degeneration on electron microscopy, together with ubiquitin-positive spheroid inclusion bodies. Purification and proteomics identified these structures as degenerating mitochondria. The mice showed autophagy and cognitive dysfunction. The authors concluded that iPLA2-gamma has an obligatory role in neuronal mitochondrial lipid metabolism and membrane structure, and that its loss of function causes a mitochondrial neurodegenerative disorder.

Saunders et al. (2015) reported a 7-year-old girl (CMH193) with a suspected mitochondrial myopathy. She was asymptomatic in her first year and met developmental milestones, although toe-walking was noted. She had a positive Gowers sign at age 2 years and could no longer walk by age 3. Her course was progressive and included proximal muscle weakness, dysmetria, dysarthria, decline in fine motor skills, oral motor dystonia, hypotonia that progressed to spasticity, complex partial seizures with left temporal lobe spikes on EEG, a very lean body habitus without weight gain, and significant lactic acidosis requiring bicarbonate supplementation.

Saunders et al. (2015) found that the patient had a persistently elevated anion gap from age 5 years. At age 7 she had elevated blood lactate (3.8-5.6 mmol/L) and pyruvate, with a lactate:pyruvate ratio that was not elevated, and a normal plasma acylcarnitine profile. CSF studies at age 6 showed 5-methyltetrahydrofolate deficiency. Creatine kinase and liver function tests were normal, mtDNA tRNA sequencing and mtDNA depletion studies were normal, and muscle SDH and COX activity and electron transport chain function were unaffected. The authors suggested this pattern indicated mitochondrial dysfunction rather than an electron transport chain defect.

Saunders et al. (2015) reported that a quadriceps muscle biopsy taken at age 4 years showed variable fiber size with isolated small atrophic type 1 and type 2 fibers, and no ragged red fibers. Electron microscopy showed mitochondria with marked disarray of the cristae, globular dense osmiophilic inclusions, and subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria with concentric lamellar membranes, suggestive of degenerating mitochondria. Secondary lysosomes containing residual bodies were increased. Brain MRI at 33 months showed subtle bilateral increased signal in the medial globus pallidus that was no longer seen 2 years later.
Increased variability in muscle fiber diameter
Subsarcolemmal accumulations of abnormally shaped mitochondria

Saunders et al. (2015) performed trio exome sequencing and found that the patient was compound heterozygous for 2 frameshift variants in the PNPLA8 gene: c.334_337delAATT (p.Asn112HisfsX29) and c.1975_1976delAG (p.Leu659AlafsX4). Both variants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Each was inherited from a carrier parent, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance, and 2 healthy sibs carried neither variant. Neither variant was present in the Exome Sequencing Project database or in an internal database of 1,913 samples.

Saunders et al. (2015) performed Western blot analysis on the patient's muscle and found a marked decrease in the 88-, 63-, and 52-kD PNPLA8 (iPLA2-gamma) protein bands compared with 3 control muscles. A 110-kD band present in controls was also absent; mass spectrometry identified this band as HSPA4, which the authors concluded had reacted nonspecifically with the antibody.

Saunders et al. (2015) noted that the patient's phenotype and mitochondrial ultrastructural abnormalities closely resembled those of Pnpla8-null mice. These mice have mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired learning, decreased exercise endurance, a thin body habitus, and cold intolerance, as well as dysmorphic mitochondria in the myocardium and cerebellum. The authors suggested that this resemblance supported a causal link between the PNPLA8 variants and the patient's disease.

Saunders et al. (2015) suggested that, as in PLA2G6-related disease, PNPLA8-related disease may result primarily from altered mitochondrial inner membrane homeostasis, with effects on electron transport and ATP synthesis being secondary.

Saunders et al. (2015) reported that the patient's symptoms initially improved with a multivitamin containing iron, carbidopa-levodopa, and leucovorin. CoQ10 supplementation increased her appetite but did not lead to weight gain.

Shukla et al. (2018) reported an Indian girl (patient 1) born to consanguineous parents. She had congenital microcephaly (head circumference -4 SD at birth) and multifocal clonic seizures starting on day 2 of life, along with spasticity of all four limbs. Brain MRI showed microcephaly with a simplified gyral pattern, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, a prominent cisterna magna with a hypoplastic cerebellum, and brainstem atrophy. MR spectroscopy showed an elevated lipid-lactate peak. TORCH testing was negative.
Elevated brain lactate level by MRS

Shukla et al. (2018) reported a girl (patient 2) of Indian/Fijian origin born to nonconsanguineous parents. She developed normally until about 13 months of age and then regressed, with epilepsia partialis continua and focal seizures. She went on to have severe developmental stagnation and acquired microcephaly (-4.7 SD at age 15 years), and she was nonverbal and fed by gastrostomy tube. She also had hypotonia, proximal muscle weakness, absent reflexes, choreiform movements, dystonia and contractures. Progressive atrophy of the cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem developed, MR spectroscopy showed a persistently elevated lipid-lactate peak, and she had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with subaortic stenosis, abnormal visual evoked potentials, obstructive sleep apnea, elevated blood lactate and elevated GDF15.

Shukla et al. (2018) found that patient 2's muscle biopsy showed enlarged, irregularly shaped mitochondria with surrounding membrane whorls, disrupted cristae, electron-dense deposits, lipid droplets and glycogen pools. Activities of electron transport chain complexes I through IV were normal. GDF15 was elevated at 1293 pg/ml at age 14 years.
Decreased activity of mitochondrial respiratory chain

Using whole-exome sequencing, Shukla et al. (2018) identified a homozygous nonsense variant in PNPLA8, c.517G>T (p.Glu173Ter; NM_001256007.1), in patient 1, the daughter of consanguineous Indian parents. Sanger sequencing confirmed that both parents were heterozygous for the variant.

Using trio whole-exome sequencing, Shukla et al. (2018) identified compound heterozygous variants in PNPLA8 in patient 2. One was a frameshift variant, c.2275_2276delCT (p.Leu759AlafsTer4), and the other was a nonsense variant, c.419C>A (p.Ser140Ter). Sanger sequencing confirmed the variants, and each was inherited from a carrier parent.
Shukla et al. (2018) found that the biallelic PNPLA8 variants were inherited from carrier parents, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

Shukla et al. (2018) noted that the 3 known patients with PNPLA8 loss-of-function variants had similar but variable clinical features. Because so few patients were known, they could not establish a genotype-phenotype correlation.

Shukla et al. (2018) noted that all the PNPLA8 variants reported so far introduce premature stop codons and are likely to cause truncated protein or nonsense-mediated decay. They also observed that the abnormal mitochondria with concentric lamellar membranes seen in patient 2 resembled findings in Pnpla8-null mice, and that the human phenotype resembled the progressive neurodegeneration seen in those mice.
Masih et al. (2021) reported a patient with severe neurodegeneration that began before birth, progressed, and led to death in infancy.

In a patient with severe neurodegeneration that began before birth, Masih et al. (2021) used whole-exome sequencing to find a novel homozygous missense variant, c.1874A>G, in the patatin domain of the PNPLA8 gene.

Burnyte et al. (2023) described 2 adult Lithuanian siblings (a brother and sister) who had slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia and sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy with onset at age 14 years and preserved cognition. The brother, aged 49 at the time of the report, had lower-limb weakness and distal muscle atrophy, ataxia and gait disturbance, tetraparesis, absent lower-limb tendon reflexes, foot deformities, bilateral Babinski signs, dysmetria, and mild distal hypoesthesia. He became nonambulant at age 44 years. At age 45 he had mild dysarthria, horizontal nystagmus, and a normal Mini-Mental State Examination score, and brain MRI showed mild cerebellar atrophy. His sister had severe axial ataxia, appendicular dysmetria, distal muscle atrophy, areflexia, and bilateral Babinski signs at age 21. EMG showed no myopathic changes.

In 2 siblings with adolescent-onset cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy, Burnyte et al. (2023) used whole-exome sequencing to identify compound heterozygous frameshift variants in exon 11 of the PNPLA8 gene: a novel c.2269del (p.Thr757GlnfsTer10) and a previously reported c.2275_2276del (p.Leu759AlafsTer4). The c.2269del variant was not found in the ExAC, 1000 Genomes, or gnomAD databases. The c.2275_2276del variant was inherited from the mother. Paternal DNA was not available, but sequencing showed that the 2 variants were on different alleles (in trans), and Sanger sequencing confirmed both variants in the affected sister.

Burnyte et al. (2023) noted that c.2275_2276del had previously been reported in compound heterozygous state with another truncating variant in a patient with severe early-childhood neurodegeneration, whereas their patients had a milder phenotype. Because both truncating variants in their patients lie in the last coding exon of PNPLA8, the authors suggested that these transcripts may escape nonsense-mediated decay and possibly retain partial enzyme activity.

Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) reported 3 patients from 2 families with PNPLA8-related mitochondriopathy. Patient 1 (Family I) had the congenital form of the disease. Patients 2 and 3 (Family II) had progressive microcephaly, seizures starting in infancy, progressive cortical atrophy, loss of white matter, bilateral degeneration of the basal ganglia, and cystic encephalomalacia.

In Patient 1 (Family I), who had the congenital form of PNPLA8-related mitochondriopathy, Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) used exome sequencing to identify a loss-of-function variant in the PNPLA8 gene, c.1231C>T (p.Arg411Ter).
In Patients 2 and 3 (Family II), who had infantile-onset disease, Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) used exome sequencing to identify a missense variant in the PNPLA8 gene, c.1559T>A (p.Val520Asp).

Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) proposed infantile onset as a new, distinct phenotype of PNPLA8-related disease. They suggested that age at disease onset correlates strongly with where the variant lies, not with what type of variant it is. They described the PNPLA8-related conditions as a spectrum of overlapping features that line up with different ages of onset.

Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) noted that only 6 patients with biallelic PNPLA8 variants had been reported before. Reported phenotypes were a congenital form (congenital microcephaly, early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, and early death), a childhood neurodegeneration form with progressive microcephaly, and an adult-onset form with cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy.

Nakamura et al. (2024) reported 14 individuals (6 male, 8 female) from 12 unrelated families, many consanguineous and from countries including Japan, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Turkey, Lebanon, Egypt and Iran, who had neurological disease and biallelic PNPLA8 variants. Age at last assessment ranged from 3 days to 33 years. Frequent features were central hypotonia (13/13), dystonia (8/12), seizures (10/14) and cerebellar atrophy (12/12).

Nakamura et al. (2024) described 8 patients (Families 1-8) at the severe end of the spectrum. They had congenital microcephaly (5/7), global developmental delay with no milestones attained (7/7), peripheral spasticity (7/8) and seizure onset within 7 months of age (8/8). Neuroimaging showed a simplified gyral pattern (6/6), pontocerebellar hypoplasia (7/7) and severe progressive cerebral cortical atrophy (5/5).

Nakamura et al. (2024) described 4 patients (Families 11-12) with a relatively mild phenotype. All learned to walk (4/4) and then lost milestones (4/4); 3 of 4 had ataxia and 3 of 4 had mild or no intellectual disability, and seizures were unique or absent. Brain MRI showed little or no cerebral cortical volume loss but progressive cerebellar atrophy. Two further patients (Families 9 and 10) were of intermediate severity.

Nakamura et al. (2024) found 14 PNPLA8 variants, 12 of them novel, by exome or genome sequencing with Sanger segregation analysis. They comprised 4 nonsense, 5 frameshift, 3 intronic variants near exon-intron boundaries and 2 missense variants. Every variant had a frequency below 0.001% in population databases (dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, jMorp and gnomAD), and 12 of the 14 individuals carried combinations of nonsense, frameshift and splice-site variants, suggesting loss of function.

In Patient 1 (Family 1), Nakamura et al. (2024) found the PNPLA8 intronic variant c.1625+3_1625+6del. In patient lymphoblastoid cells it caused skipping of exons 6-8 through aberrant splicing, and the patient's fibroblasts showed a significant reduction of the 77-kDa PNPLA8 protein, indicating a null effect.

Nakamura et al. (2024) found the PNPLA8 splice-acceptor variants c.2075-2A>G in Patient 2 and c.1684-2A>G in Patient 5. No patient cells were available, but SpliceAI predicted loss of the splice acceptor site, with delta scores of 0.97 and 0.93, respectively.

In Patient 6, who had a severe phenotype, Nakamura et al. (2024) found the PNPLA8 frameshift variant p.Glu296Lysfs*6. Like Patient 1's variant, it resulted in a null effect on PNPLA8 protein in skin fibroblasts.

Nakamura et al. (2024) combined their patients with 11 previously reported individuals from 8 families and found that biallelic loss-of-function variants affecting 3 or 4 PNPLA8 protein isoforms were associated with the severe phenotype. Patients with a relatively mild neurodegenerative phenotype with late-onset movement disorders all carried biallelic C-terminal frameshift variants (p.Thr757Glnfs*10 or p.Leu759Alafs*4). Intermediate cases carried a loss-of-function variant, missense variants or the recurrent p.Leu759Alafs*4.

In skin fibroblasts, Nakamura et al. (2024) found weak residual expression of the 77-kDa PNPLA8 protein in Patient 12 (mild phenotype, p.Leu759Alafs*4) and in Patient 14 (non-neuronal phenotype, p.Val7*). In contrast, the homozygous missense variant p.Val520Asp from a previously reported patient with a severe phenotype gave protein levels similar to controls. The authors suggested that C-terminal truncating variants escape nonsense-mediated decay, leading to less severe disease.

In 2 unrelated Iranian families from a non-neurological cohort, Nakamura et al. (2024) identified individuals homozygous for distinct N-terminal PNPLA8 frameshift variants that affect only the largest (88-kDa) isoform. One proband had optic atrophy and the other had nonsyndromic hearing loss. In the optic atrophy family, an affected sib was only heterozygous for the variant, so the authors considered these variants of undetermined significance.

In skin fibroblasts from Patient 1, Nakamura et al. (2024) found significantly lower maximal mitochondrial respiration than in healthy controls, although mitochondrial morphology was normal on electron microscopy. Cardiolipin and monolysocardiolipin appeared decreased in patient fibroblasts compared with controls but did not correlate with phenotypic severity.

Nakamura et al. (2024) made cerebral organoids from CRISPR/Cas9 PNPLA8-knockout human iPSCs and from iPSCs of Patient 1. These organoids had a smaller subventricular zone-like region, fewer PAX6+HOPX+ basal radial glial cells and fewer SATB2+ upper-layer neurons, while deep-layer neurons and basal intermediate progenitors were unchanged. Knockout neural progenitors had normal mitochondrial morphology and respiration but reduced lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), lysophosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidic acid, and adding LPA partly restored the number of basal radial glia in patient organoids.
